title: took me 2 months of prompting for both code and graphics. Any potentials?
author: Square-Yam-3772
selftext:
I have been incorporating ai into my gamedev previously before (for small jam submissions) but this is my most recent project. Took me 2 months of prompting Chatgpt

https://reddit.com/link/1otzast/video/ki8qf0dpuj0g1/player

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/2980350/Spacelane\_Express/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2980350/Spacelane_Express/)

Please leave a comment if you have any questions. I am happy to share my experience here. Thanks

comments.author: KrombopulusMikeKills
comments.body: looks really good. are you a programmer or did you prompt this as a non-programmer?

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
I come from a coding background and I prompt Chatgpt as though it is another developer working with me. Most of my prompts are just requirements e.g. I want the player to be able to do this or I need this mechanic in my project. I did occasionally have to troubleshoot bugs myself but Chatgpt helps a ton. It also helps a lot to be specific. 

the scary thing I noticed in the recent months is that Chatgpt seems to know it needs more details to respond better i.e. it literally would ask me for screenshot so it can "see" what I see...

replies.author: KrombopulusMikeKills
replies.body: thats crazy. do you use an engine and make chatgpt program for it, or is it with no engine at all?

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
I used an engine. From my experience with my other project, I found it taking too long to prompt everything from scratch. Chatgpt can get confused or I get confused as the project grows. 

I have been a long time Unity3d user so it makes sense for me to start from there. Chatgpt has no problem dealing with Unity3d projects so it works out pretty well. The only issue I found is that it sometimes use outdated syntax. If I complain, Chatgpt would fix it but it seems to prefer doing things a certain way. Its weird but I find it best not to get into too many revisions with Chatgpt

replies.author: KrombopulusMikeKills
replies.body: thats an interesting tip, not to revise. for a non-coder, what do you think is the best way to go about ai creating a game? im guessing using unity would be bad because its another layer of complexity that a non-coder doesnt know how to use

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
revisions are still necessary but I would avoid excessive revisions: 

* maybe its just my browser issue, but the chatgpt thread would get sluggish once the page gets too long. Start a new chat works but chatgpt's memory can get iffy (I just went with default memory settings)
* chatgpt can go in circles sometimes
* chatgpt can be stubborn at times even if you prompt against certain things over and over. its best not to fight it

I personally got a crash course on shader graphs and Audacity because Chatgpt is able to hold my hand through the steps. You can actually use any tools you want, as long as you are prepare to prompt Chatgpt all the time... I have had chat where I said "I have no idea where to click" and it goes from there

I haven't personally tried this exactly but maybe start with a genre and ask Chatgpt for a fully working project. Test the project and then ask Chatgpt for more tweaks. I know for a fact that Chatgpt can crank out working python scripts, so it should be able to just give you working html5/javascript too

replies.author: agarlington
replies.body:
I just wanted to give my 2 cents since I'm going about making a game with AI as my co-dev/coder. 
Macko AI and then the rosebud AI platforms have been great for prompting ai to code a game, with no coding background. 
if you wanna make a game check them out, also wefun AI is a brand new one that's actually really impressive so far it was able to shit me out a working prototype from just "make me a top down rpg" haha pretty neat tools.

replies.author: No_Fennel_9073
replies.body:
Actually, as a Unity dev, I think Unity provides a solid framework so that if you literally know nothing, you are forced to learn: where to create a script, how to attach it to a game object, other types of components, how the Hierarchy works (child / parent component architecture), how scenes work, how UI works. It has a very visual, immediate feedback loop. The console is incredible to for logging stuff and debugging, even if you are solely using ChatGPT or whatever AI. Just prefix every debug log with “[CLASS NAME]”, use search to find that class to identify where the error is occurring.

ChatGPT is pretty smart with Unity as OP said.

I actually use Gemini though for extremely precise debugging.

comments.author: Venom4992
comments.body: This looks like a game made by one human for a week long game jam.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
it took me a week just to set up the basics and get a bug-free build.

This has peer-to-peer co-op mode by the way...

this is my 1-week long jam with maybe 50% AI assistance by comparison: [https://chooon.itch.io/necromancer-intern](https://chooon.itch.io/necromancer-intern)

do you have a recent 1-week game jam submission via AI? I would love to see it

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body: its just PVE co-op for now. My original idea is just getting my friends into a session so I can show off and give them items for fun. My older idea was making a "mmo-lite" and showing it off to my friends but a "mmo-lite" takes too long even with AI's help

comments.author: EthelUltima
comments.body:
I like the UI and colours but movement looks unrealistic? The way it rotates around doesn't make sense. From the trailer it doesn't feel like you're in space. Is there a cockpit view? I feel like it needs more immersion, doesn't capture that lone hauler vibe imo.

Not keen on EA either, puts a lot of people off. Better to release a demo and get feedback that way.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
* yeah I probably should fix that instant turning
* no cockpit view as of now
* not capturing the vibe is ummm... I need to sit on that one for a bit

I mostly just want to have the experience of putting out a EA. Do demos actually work better? I suppose I didn't do demos right before

replies.author: EthelUltima
replies.body:
Look at a game like Elite Dangerous for vibe. I think in a game about hauling the docking, loading, offloading process needs to be way more immersive rather than just menus. It is your game at end of the day though so remember to stick to your vision.

My game was entirely vibe coded in around the same timeframe and I put a demo out. 1 person who had never played the genre before left some good and back and forth feedback and it made me realise how many bad design choices I really had made.  Making any changes at that point was a mammoth task so its abandoned now essentially which is kinda sad. I really should have planned it all out better. So Demo's are good if you can get honest feedback from someone.

comments.body: Not sure why you're getting downvoted. For a fully vibe coded game this is one of the more advanced I've seen.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body: I use steam peer-to-peer networking for this so...

comments.author: vaksninus
comments.body: is there supposed to be sounds? Would help the immersion a lot if done well.

comments.author: No_Fennel_9073
comments.body:
Is this all in the browser using three.js or react three fiber? If so, that 👏👏👏

You’ve probably already done this, but I would write documentation, or get the AI, to write documentation for how all of the systems in your game work.

Use those systems that you know work to make other games.

Keep improving on them, ask AI (Gemini whatever) if there is a better approach to structure newer projects from a systems design perspective. Then you can come back to this in 6 months and refactor it without AI once you understand the different programming and game design patterns.
